Question: Within how many days must a commercial bank close a credit card after the cardholder asks for closure, and what happens if it is late?
Answer: The bank must close the card within seven working days of the request, provided all dues are paid. If it misses that deadline it must pay the cardholder a penalty of ₹500 for every calendar day of delay until the account is closed, as long as nothing is outstanding on the account.
Golden Para: 19. Any request for closure of a credit card shall be honoured within seven working days by the credit card-issuer, subject to payment of all dues by the cardholder. Subsequent to the closure of credit card, the cardholder shall be immediately notified about the closure through email, SMS, etc. Cardholders shall be provided option to submit request for closure of credit card account through multiple channels such as helpline, dedicated email-id, Interactive Voice Response (IVR), prominently visible link on the website, internet banking, mobile-app or any other mode. The card-issuer shall not insist on sending a closure request through post or any other means which may result in the delay of receipt of the request. Failure on the part of the card-issuers to complete the process of closure within seven working days shall result in a penalty of ₹500 per calendar day of delay payable to the cardholder, till the closure of the account provided there is no outstanding in the account.

Question: A bank upgraded my credit card without my consent and billed me for it. What must the bank do?
Answer: Issuing or upgrading cards without explicit consent is prohibited. The bank must immediately reverse the charges and also pay you, without dispute, a penalty equal to twice the reversed charges. You can additionally approach the RBI Ombudsman for compensation for time lost, expenses, harassment and mental anguish.
Golden Para: (4) The issue of unsolicited cards / upgradation is strictly prohibited. In case, an unsolicited card is issued / existing card upgraded and activated without the explicit consent of the recipient and the latter is billed for the same, the card-issuer shall not only reverse the charges forthwith, but also pay a penalty without demur to the recipient amounting to twice the value of the charges reversed. In addition, the person in whose name the card is issued can also approach the RBI Ombudsman who would determine the amount of compensation payable by the card-issuer to the recipient of the unsolicited card as per the provisions of the Ombudsman Scheme, i.e., for loss of complainant’s time, expenses incurred, harassment and mental anguish suffered by him / her.

Question: What happens to a bank credit card that has not been used for more than a year?
Answer: The bank starts the closure process after informing the cardholder. If the cardholder does not reply within 30 days, the bank closes the card account, subject to the cardholder paying all dues.
Golden Para: 20. If a credit card has not been used for a period of more than one year, the process to close the card shall be initiated after intimating the cardholder. If no reply is received from the cardholder within a period of 30 days, the card account shall be closed by the card-issuer, subject to payment of all dues by the cardholder.

Question: How often must a bank carry out periodic KYC updation for high, medium and low-risk customers?
Answer: At least once every two years for high-risk customers, once every eight years for medium-risk customers and once every ten years for low-risk customers, counted from account opening or the last KYC updation.
Golden Para: (1) The bank shall adopt a risk-based approach for periodic updation of KYC ensuring that it keeps the information or data collected under CDD is kept up-to-date and relevant, particularly where there is high risk. However, the bank shall carry out periodic updation at least once in every two years for high-risk customers, once in every eight years for medium risk customers and once in every 10 years for low-risk customers from the date of opening of the account / last KYC updation. The bank shall document its policy in this regard as part of the bank’s internal KYC policy duly approved by the Board of Directors of bank or any committee of the Board to which power has been delegated.

Question: For KYC purposes, what ownership level makes a person the beneficial owner of a company or a partnership firm customer?
Answer: For a company, a natural person who owns or is entitled to more than 10 percent of the shares, capital or profits (or who exercises control, such as the right to appoint a majority of directors). For a partnership firm, a natural person with more than 10 percent of capital or profits, or who exercises control through other means.
Golden Para: (a) Where the customer is a company, the beneficial owner is the natural person(s), who, whether acting alone or together, or through one or more juridical persons, has / have a controlling ownership interest or who exercises control through other means. Explanation: For the purpose of this sub-clause- • ‘Controlling ownership interest’ means ownership of / entitlement to more than 10 percent of the shares or capital or profits of the company. • ‘Control’ shall include the right to appoint the majority of the directors or to control the management or policy decisions including by virtue of their shareholding or management rights or shareholders agreements or voting agreements. (b) Where the customer is a partnership firm, the beneficial owner is the natural person(s), who, whether acting alone or together, or through one or more juridical person(s), has / have ownership of / entitlement to more than 10 percent of capital or profits of the partnership or who exercises control through other means.

Question: What transaction and balance limits apply to a bank 'Small Account'?
Answer: Total credits in a financial year cannot exceed ₹1 lakh, total withdrawals and transfers in a month cannot exceed ₹10,000, and the balance at any time cannot exceed ₹50,000. The balance limit is not applied to Government grants, welfare benefits and payments against procurements.
Golden Para: 28. Notwithstanding anything contained in paragraph 23 and as an alternative thereto, in case an individual who desires to open a bank account, the bank shall open a ‘Small Account’, which entails the following limitations: (1) the aggregate of all credits in a financial year does not exceed Rupees One Lakh; (2) the aggregate of all withdrawals and transfers in a month does not exceed ₹10,000; and (3) the balance at any point of time does not exceed ₹50,000. Provided that the bank shall not consider this limit on balance when making deposits through Government grants, welfare benefits and payment against procurements.

Question: After a borrower fully repays a personal loan, how quickly must the bank return the original property documents, and what compensation applies if it is late?
Answer: The bank must release all original movable or immovable property documents and remove registered charges within 30 days of full repayment or settlement. If the delay is attributable to the bank, it must compensate the borrower at ₹5,000 for each day of delay.
Golden Para: 354. A bank shall release all the original movable / immovable property documents and remove charges registered with any registry within a period of 30 days after full repayment / settlement of the loan account. 355. A borrower shall be given the option of collecting the original movable / immovable property documents either from the banking outlet / branch where the loan account was serviced or any other office of the bank where the documents are available, as per her / his preference. 356.The timeline and place of return of original movable / immovable property documents shall be mentioned in the loan sanction letters issued on or after December 01, 2023. 357. In order to address the contingent event of demise of the sole borrower or joint borrowers, a bank shall have a well laid out procedure for return of original movable / immovable property documents to the legal heir(s). Such procedure shall be displayed on the website of the bank along with other similar policies and procedures for customer information. F.2 Compensation for delay in release of Property Documents 358. A bank shall communicate to the borrower reasons for delay in releasing of original movable / immovable property documents or failing to file charge satisfaction form with relevant registry beyond 30 days after full repayment / settlement of loan. In case where the delay is attributable to the bank, it shall compensate the borrower at the rate of ₹5,000 for each day of delay.

Question: Within how many days must a bank settle a claim on a deceased customer's deposit account, and what compensation is due if the bank delays?
Answer: Within 15 calendar days of receiving all required documents. If the delay is attributable to the bank, it must pay interest of at least the prevailing Bank Rate plus 4 per cent per annum on the settlement amount for the period of delay.
Golden Para: 319. A bank shall settle a claim in respect of deposit accounts of a deceased customer within a period not exceeding 15 calendar days from the date of receipt of all the required documents associated with the claim. 320. In case of safe deposit locker / articles in safe custody, the bank shall, within 15 calendar days of receipt of all the required documents, process the claim and communicate with the claimant(s) for fixing the date for making inventory of the locker / articles in safe custody. E.5 Compensation for delay in settlement of claims 321. If any deposit related claim is not settled within the timeframe stipulated at paragraph 319 above, then a bank shall communicate the reasons for such delay to the claimant(s). Further, in cases of delay attributable to the bank, compensation shall be paid by the bank in the form of interest, at a rate not less than the prevailing Bank Rate + 4 per cent per annum, on the settlement amount due for the period of delay.

Question: For a deceased customer's safe deposit locker, what is the bank's timeline and what compensation applies if it misses it?
Answer: Within 15 calendar days of receiving all required documents, the bank must process the claim and contact the claimants to fix a date for the locker inventory. If it misses this timeline it must pay the claimants ₹5,000 for each day of delay.
Golden Para:
320. In case of safe deposit locker / articles in safe custody, the bank shall, within 15 calendar days of receipt of all the required documents, process the claim and communicate with the claimant(s) for fixing the date for making inventory of the locker / articles in safe custody.
…
322. For claims related to safe deposit locker / articles in safe custody, the bank shall be required to pay compensation to the claimant(s) at the rate of ₹5,000 for each day of delay, in cases where it doesn’t adhere to the timeline prescribed in paragraph 320 above.

Question: When does a customer have zero liability for an unauthorised electronic banking transaction?
Answer: When the fraud results from contributory fraud, negligence or deficiency on the bank's part (whether or not the customer reports it), or when it is a third-party breach with no fault of either bank or customer and the customer notifies the bank within three working days of receiving the bank's communication about the transaction.
Golden Para: 67. A customer’s entitlement to zero liability shall arise where the unauthorised transaction occurs in the following events: (1) Contributory fraud / negligence / deficiency on the part of the bank (irrespective of whether the transaction is reported by the customer or not). (2) Third party breach where the deficiency lies neither with the bank nor with the customer but lies elsewhere in the system, and the customer notifies the bank within three working days of receiving the communication from the bank regarding the unauthorised transaction.

Question: What counts as a 'bulk deposit' for a commercial bank?
Answer: A single rupee term deposit of ₹3 crore and above.
Golden Para: (2) ‘Bulk Deposit’ means Single Rupee term deposits of ₹3 crore and above.

Question: Can a bank offer an individual a ₹50 lakh term deposit without a premature withdrawal option?
Answer: No. Banks may offer term deposits without a premature withdrawal option, but all term deposits from individuals (held singly or jointly) of ₹1 crore and below must have a premature withdrawal facility, so a ₹50 lakh deposit must allow it.
Golden Para: (3) Non-availability of premature withdrawal option A bank shall have the freedom to offer term deposits without premature withdrawal option. Provided that all term deposits accepted by a bank from individuals (held singly or jointly) for amount of ₹1 crore and below shall have premature withdrawal facility.

Question: How often must interest on an external-benchmark-linked loan be reset?
Answer: At least once in three months.
Golden Para: 38. The interest rate under external benchmark shall be reset at least once in three months.

Question: What is the 'cooling-off period' for a bank's digital loan and how long must it be?
Answer: It is an initial period during which the borrower can exit the digital loan by paying the principal and the proportionate APR without any penalty. The bank sets the period in its credit policy, but it cannot be less than one day. The bank may keep a reasonable one-time processing fee if this is disclosed upfront in the KFS.
Golden Para: 11. Cooling-off period (1) The borrower shall be given an explicit option to exit a digital loan by paying the principal and the proportionate APR without any penalty during an initial “cooling-off period”. The cooling off period shall be determined by the bank in terms of its credit policy, subject to the period so determined not being less than one day. For borrower continuing with the loan even after cooling-off period, pre-payment shall continue to be allowed as per the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025. (2) The bank may retain a reasonable one-time processing fee, if the customer exits the loan during the cooling-off period. This, if applicable, shall be disclosed to the customer upfront in KFS.

Question: For what period can an NBFC accept a public deposit?
Answer: The deposit must be repayable after at least twelve months and no later than sixty months from the date of acceptance or renewal.
Golden Para: 16. No NBFC shall accept or renew any public deposit, unless such deposit is repayable after a period of twelve months but not later than sixty months from the date of acceptance or renewal thereof.

Question: What is the maximum interest rate an NBFC can pay on public deposits?
Answer: Twelve and a half per cent per annum. Interest can be paid or compounded at rests no shorter than monthly.
Golden Para: 19. No NBFC shall invite or accept or renew public deposit at a rate of interest exceeding twelve and half per cent per annum. Interest may be paid or compounded at rests which shall not be shorter than monthly rests.

Question: Two months after placing a public deposit with an NBFC, can the depositor withdraw it early or borrow against it?
Answer: No. NBFCs cannot repay a public deposit prematurely or lend against it within the three-month lock-in period from acceptance, except on the depositor's death (and the emergency provisions for tiny deposits). After three months, an NBFC that is not a problem NBFC may lend up to 75 per cent of the deposit at two percentage points above the deposit rate.
Golden Para:
35. No NBFC shall grant any loan against a public deposit or make premature repayment of a public deposit within a period of three months (lock-in period) from the date of its acceptance:
…
(2) grant a loan up to 75 per cent of the amount of public deposit to a depositor after the expiry of three months from the date of deposit at a rate of interest two percentage points above the interest rate payable on the deposit.

Question: What does an NBFC need before it can issue credit cards?
Answer: Prior approval from the Reserve Bank, a Certificate of Registration and specific permission for the business. The prerequisite is a minimum net owned fund of ₹100 crore, plus any conditions RBI specifies.
Golden Para: 7. Non-Banking Financial Companies registered with the Reserve Bank shall not undertake credit card business without prior approval of the Reserve Bank. Any company including a non-deposit taking company intending to engage in this activity shall require a Certificate of Registration, apart from specific permission to enter into this business, the pre-requisite for which is a minimum net owned fund of ₹100 crore and subject to such terms and conditions as the Reserve Bank may specify in this regard from time to time. Without obtaining prior approval from the Reserve Bank, NBFCs shall not issue, credit cards, charge cards, or similar products virtually or physically.

Question: How much gold or silver can a borrower pledge with a bank for loans?
Answer: Across all loans to a borrower: up to 1 kilogram of gold ornaments or 10 kilograms of silver ornaments, and up to 50 grams of gold coins or 500 grams of silver coins.
Golden Para: 40. Loans against ornaments and coins shall be subject to the following: (1) The aggregate weight of ornaments pledged for all loans to a borrower shall not exceed 1 kilogram for gold ornaments, and 10 kilograms for silver ornaments. (2) The aggregate weight of coin(s) pledged for all loans to a borrower shall not exceed 50 grams in case of gold coins, and 500 grams in case of silver coins.

Question: What provision must a bank hold on an unsecured exposure classified as substandard?
Answer: 25 per cent of the outstanding balance: the general 15 per cent substandard provision plus an additional 10 per cent for unsecured exposures.
Golden Para: 85. A general provision of 15 per cent on total outstanding shall be made in respect of substandard assets without making any allowance for Export Credit Guarantee Corporation (ECGC) guarantee cover and securities available. 86. The ‘unsecured exposures’ which are identified as ‘substandard’ shall attract additional provision of 10 per cent, i.e., a total of 25 per cent on the outstanding balance

Question: A customer with a ₹3 lakh credit card limit reports a third-party fraud on the sixth working day after being alerted. What is the most they can be made to pay per transaction?
Answer: ₹10,000 or the transaction value, whichever is lower. Reporting within four to seven working days of a third-party breach caps liability at the Table 1 amount, and credit cards with limits up to ₹5 lakh fall in the ₹10,000 band.

(2) In cases where the responsibility for the unauthorised electronic banking transaction lies neither with the bank nor with the customer, but lies elsewhere in the system and the customer notifies the bank of such a transaction within four to seven working days of receiving a communication of the transaction, the per transaction liability of the customer shall be limited to the transaction value or the amount mentioned in Table 1, whichever is lower.

Question: What is the maximum loan-to-value ratio for a ₹4 lakh consumption loan against gold jewellery from a bank?
Answer: 80 per cent. Consumption loans above ₹2.5 lakh and up to ₹5 lakh per borrower are capped at an 80 per cent LTV, and the ratio must be maintained throughout the loan's tenor.

Question: An advance has been in the 'doubtful' category for two years. What provision must the bank hold on its secured portion?
Answer: 40 per cent of the secured portion, since the asset has been doubtful for one to three years. The portion not covered by the realisable value of security needs 100 per cent provision.

Question: A borrower's likely loss from unhedged foreign currency exposure is 40 per cent of its EBID. What extra provision must the bank make?
Answer: An incremental 40 basis points on its total credit exposures to that borrower, over and above the standard asset provision, because 40 per cent falls in the 'more than 30 and up to 50 per cent' band.

Question: An MSE takes an ₹80 lakh floating-rate business loan in 2026 and wants to prepay it. Can a commercial bank charge a pre-payment fee? Can an NBFC?
Answer: A commercial bank cannot levy any pre-payment charges on floating-rate business loans to individuals and MSEs sanctioned on or after 1 January 2026. For NBFCs it depends on the layer: an NBFC-Upper Layer cannot charge, and an NBFC-Middle Layer is barred only for loans up to ₹50 lakh. For an ₹80 lakh loan from an NBFC-ML (or another NBFC), charges may apply under its approved policy.
Golden Para:
(2) For all floating rate loans granted for business purpose to individuals and MSEs, with or without co-obligant(s), a bank shall not levy any pre-payment charges.
…
(2) For all floating rate loans granted for business purpose to individuals and Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs), as defined in Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (MSMED) Act, 2006, with or without co-obligant(s): (i) an NBFC-Upper Layer shall not levy any pre-payment charges. (ii) an NBFC-Middle Layer shall not levy any pre-payment charges on loans with sanctioned amount/ limit up to ₹50 lakh.

Question: What is the shortest term deposit a commercial bank can offer, compared with the shortest public deposit an NBFC can accept?
Answer: A commercial bank's minimum deposit tenor is seven days. An NBFC public deposit must be for at least twelve months (and at most sixty months).
Golden Para:
(1) Tenor of deposits A bank shall have the freedom to determine the maturity / tenor of the deposit subject to the condition that minimum tenor of the deposit offered shall be seven days.
…
16. No NBFC shall accept or renew any public deposit, unless such deposit is repayable after a period of twelve months but not later than sixty months from the date of acceptance or renewal thereof.

Question: Today a commercial bank is classifying NPAs and making provisions. Which Direction applies: the 2025 IRACP Directions or the 2026 Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition Directions?
Answer: The 2025 Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning Directions still apply. The 2026 Directions come into force only from 1 April 2027, and the 2025 Directions will be repealed at that point.
Golden Para: 2. These Directions shall come into force with effect from April 1, 2027. 3. Banks shall continue to be governed by the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 until the date of commencement of these Directions. On such commencement, the said Directions shall stand repealed.

Question: Under the 2026 Asset Classification Directions, when does a credit card account become an NPA, and from when does this rule apply?
Answer: A credit card account becomes an NPA when the minimum amount due on the statement is not paid in full within 90 days of the payment due date. The rule is in the 2026 Directions, which take effect from 1 April 2027 (see paras 2–3 of the same Direction).
Golden Para: (7) A credit card account where the minimum amount due, as mentioned in the statement, is not paid fully within ninety days from the payment due date mentioned in the statement

Answer: Not in corpus. None of the indexed Directions states a CRAR requirement; it would be in the Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy Directions, which is not part of this corpus. The copilot should say so rather than guess.
